data_source: LOCA2 (Pierce et al., 2023) statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution, processed through the Monthly Water Balance Model (MWBM) developed by Jay Alder (Alder & USGS 2023)
methodology: Percent change in mean annual water availability (runoff) between historical and future periods, using the 10th percentile (p10) value across all 72 climate projections (27 GCMs x 3 SSPs = 72 GCM-SSP combinations). The p10 represents a plausible dry-end scenario consistent with precautionary water supply planning. Values are spatially averaged in a 3x3 grid cell window around the water supply grid cell; the model combination closest to the p10 of the percent-change distribution is selected. This value is then weighted by the percentage of climate projections predicting a decrease in mean annual water supply as a measure of confidence in the predicted risk.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative change (decreased water availability) = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2/MWBM (see Change in Runoff)
methodology: Percentage of all 72 climate projections predicting a decrease in mean annual water availability (runoff). High model agreement provides confidence that projected declines are robust. This value is applied as a 0-1 confidence weight on Change in Runoff rather than entering the score as an independent axis.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher % = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 (Pierce et al., 2023) statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution, processed through the Monthly Water Balance Model (MWBM) developed by Jay Alder (Alder & USGS 2023)
methodology: Change in the circular center of runoff timing between the historical and future periods, expressed as the number of days shifted. Monthly runoff is spatially averaged across the 3x3 grid-cell neighborhood surrounding each water supply, and a runoff-weighted center of timing is calculated for each complete water year and GCM x SSP combination on a circular October-September calendar. The direction supported by the most model realizations is selected: the 10th-percentile value is used when earlier timing is dominant and the 90th-percentile value when later timing is dominant. The absolute magnitude of the selected shift is used as the indicator, because both earlier and later shifts can disrupt established seasonal supply patterns. PROVISIONAL: the methodology for this indicator is still under revision and its scores are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger absolute timing shift = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2/MWBM (see Change in Runoff Timing)
methodology: Fraction (0-1) of climate projections supporting the selected direction of timing change. This value is applied as a confidence weight on Change in Runoff Timing rather than entering the score as an independent axis. PROVISIONAL: inherits the development status of the timing indicator it weights.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher agreement = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 (Pierce et al., 2023) statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution, processed through the Monthly Water Balance Model (MWBM) developed by Jay Alder (Alder & USGS 2023)
methodology: Percent change in mean annual water availability (precipitation, used for rainwater-based supplies) between historical and future periods, using the 10th percentile (p10) value across all 72 climate projections. Values are spatially averaged in a 3x3 grid cell window around the water supply grid cell; the model combination closest to the p10 of the percent-change distribution is selected. This value is then weighted by the percentage of climate projections predicting a decrease in mean annual precipitation as a measure of confidence in the predicted risk.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative change (decreased water availability) = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2/MWBM (see Change in Precipitation)
methodology: Percentage of all 72 climate projections predicting a decrease in mean annual water availability (precipitation, for rainwater-based supplies). This value is applied as a 0-1 confidence weight on Change in Precipitation rather than entering the score as an independent axis.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher % = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 (Pierce et al., 2023) statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution, processed through the Monthly Water Balance Model (MWBM) developed by Jay Alder (Alder & USGS 2023)
methodology: Change in the circular center of precipitation timing between the historical and future periods, expressed as the number of days shifted. Monthly precipitation is spatially averaged across the 3x3 grid-cell neighborhood surrounding each water supply, and a precipitation-weighted center of timing is calculated for each complete water year and GCM x SSP combination on a circular October-September calendar. The direction supported by the most model realizations is selected, and the absolute magnitude of that shift is used as the indicator. PROVISIONAL: the methodology for this indicator is still under revision and its scores are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger absolute timing shift = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2/MWBM (see Change in Precipitation Timing)
methodology: Fraction (0-1) of climate projections supporting the selected direction of timing change. This value is applied as a confidence weight on Change in Precipitation Timing rather than entering the score as an independent axis. PROVISIONAL: inherits the development status of the timing indicator it weights.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher agreement = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023)
methodology: Change in mean SPEI (Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index) between historical and future periods, using the 10th percentile (p10) value across climate projections. SPEI is calculated from monthly climatic water balance (precipitation minus PET) using a 12-month accumulation scale. Mean SPEI is calculated for each historical and future period by GCM-SSP-run combination, and the model combination closest to the p10 of the SPEI-change distribution is selected. Infinite SPEI values are capped at +/-4 before averaging.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative values (drier conditions) = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 (see Change in Drought)
methodology: Percentage of climate projections predicting a decrease in SPEI between the historical and future periods. High model agreement indicates greater confidence that projected drying is robust across the ensemble. This value is applied as a 0-1 confidence weight on Change in Drought rather than entering the score as an independent axis.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher % = more vulnerable

data_source: USGS observed water use data for historical withdrawals; Warziniack et al. (2022) projected water demand for future withdrawals
methodology: Percent change in mean annual county-level water withdrawals between the historical period (1985-2015) and the future period (2035-2065). Total withdrawals are summed across major water-use sectors (aquaculture, domestic, industrial and mining, irrigated agriculture, livestock, thermoelectric). The 90th percentile value across 20 future demand scenarios (5 GCMs x 4 SSP/RCP futures) is used to represent a plausible high-demand outcome.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher increase = more vulnerable

data_source: USGS / Warziniack et al. (2022) (see Change in Competition)
methodology: Percentage of future demand scenarios projecting an increase in mean annual county-level water withdrawals relative to the historical period. This value is applied as a 0-1 confidence weight on Change in Competition rather than entering the score as an independent axis.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher % = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2/MWBM historical and future runoff/precipitation projections (Pierce et al. 2023; Alder & USGS 2023); projected park-level visitation from PRISM-trained, LOCA2-driven visitation models; NPS Visitor Use Statistics
methodology: Monthly supply and monthly visitation are each converted to annual shares so that each 12-month curve sums to 1, placing supply and demand on a comparable unitless scale. The timing mismatch score is the area under the curve (AUC) where the visitation share exceeds the supply share. The indicator is future AUC minus historical AUC, summarized using the 90th percentile across paired climate/visitation projections to represent a plausible high-mismatch outcome, then weighted by the percentage of future scenarios in which future mismatch AUC exceeds historical AUC. PROVISIONAL: the methodology for this indicator is still under revision and its scores are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger increase in mismatch = more vulnerable

data_source: NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer inundation extent rasters matched to Interagency Sea Level Rise Task Force (ITF) 83rd-percentile 2050 sea level projections (Sweet et al., 2022)
methodology: Percentage-point change in inundated area within the 4 km water supply buffer between the present-day surface and the NOAA inundation depth increment nearest to each site's ITF 83rd-percentile SLR projection. Non-coastal sites receive NA and contribute 0 to the Euclidean distance calculation.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher inundation change = more vulnerable

data_source: Adams et al. (2024) global saltwater intrusion migration dataset, combined with distance to coast
methodology: Each water supply is assigned the projected saltwater-freshwater interface migration due to recharge change and sea level rise out to 2100 from the nearest available coastal watershed centroid. This value is divided by the water supply's distance to coast to provide a unitless ratio of the fraction of the corridor intruded, capped at 1. Water supplies farther than 50 km from any SWI estimation point are assigned NA.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher ratio (greater fraction of the corridor intruded) = more vulnerable

data_source: Muis et al. (2023) 100-year return period (RP100) storm surge projections, combined with distance to coast
methodology: Each water supply is assigned the worst-case (largest) change in RP100 storm surge level across the 4-model ensemble at its nearest surge station, divided by the water supply's distance to the coast to weight exposure by coastal proximity. Water supplies farther than 50 km from any surge station are assigned NA. PROVISIONAL: the methodology for this indicator is still under revision and its scores are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger surge increase = more vulnerable

data_source: Gao et al. (2021) pyrome-level fire probability projections based on an ensemble of statistically downscaled CMIP5 GCMs combined with the Physical Chemistry Fire Frequency Model (PC2FM); 20 GCMs x 2 RCP scenarios (RCP4.5, RCP8.5)
methodology: Percent change in annual fire probability from baseline (1971-2000) to mid-century (2040-2069) at the 90th percentile (p90) across all 40 climate projections for the water supply's pyrome. The p90 represents a plausible high-risk fire scenario. This value is then weighted by the percentage of projections predicting an increase in fire probability.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher projected increase = more vulnerable

data_source: Gao et al. (2021) (see Change in Fire Probability)
methodology: Percentage of the 40 climate projections predicting an increase in annual fire probability for the water supply's pyrome. This value is applied as a 0-1 confidence weight on Change in Fire Probability rather than entering the score as an independent axis.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher % = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled temperature projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023), processed for the water-supply locations using the LOCA2/MWBM data products (Alder & USGS 2023)
methodology: Difference in mean annual air temperature between the historical and future periods, using the 90th percentile value across the GCM-SSP projections (SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5). Values are spatially averaged across a 3x3 grid cell window surrounding each water supply, annual means are calculated for each GCM-SSP combination, and the modeled value closest to the p90 of the temperature-change distribution is selected. Air temperature is a proxy for warming pressure on the system, not a measurement of source-water temperature, which is unavailable nationally. PROVISIONAL: the methodology for this indicator is still under revision and its scores are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: greater projected warming = more vulnerable

data_source: NPS Public Use Statistics (1990-2024)
methodology: Sen's slope (Sen, 1968) of annual recreation visitor counts, scaled as annual percent change relative to each park's long-term mean visitation. Significance assessed with the Mann-Kendall trend test (Mann, 1945; Kendall, 1975). Parks with fewer than 3 years of data receive NA.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: increasing trend = more pressure = more vulnerable

data_source: USGS County-Level Water Withdrawal Data, 1985-2015 (USFS RPA compilation)
methodology: Sen's slope of total county-level water withdrawals across all major sectors (domestic, industrial, irrigated agriculture, aquaculture, livestock, thermoelectric). Each water supply is assigned to its nearest county via spatial join. Withdrawals are normalized by county area (Mgal/day/km2) before trend estimation.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: increasing regional demand = more competition = more vulnerable

data_source: MWBM historical runoff and precipitation data (Alder & USGS 2023); NPS Visitor Use Statistics historical recreation visitation data
methodology: Monthly water availability and monthly visitation are summarized over the historical period (1984-2014). Water availability is represented by runoff for groundwater, spring and surface-water supplies and by precipitation for rainwater-harvesting supplies. Supply and visitation are each converted to monthly shares of their annual total, and the indicator is the area under the curve (AUC) where monthly visitation share exceeds monthly water supply share. Because both curves sum to 1, the score describes seasonal alignment, not whether total annual supply meets total annual demand. PROVISIONAL: the methodology for this indicator is still under revision and its scores are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger mismatch area = more vulnerable

data_source: NPS Water Supply Database (recorded well depth); Ma et al. (2026) machine-learning water table depth model (~30 m resolution, CONUS)
methodology: For groundwater- and spring-sourced supplies, depth to water is taken from the WSD's recorded well depth, assumed to sit at 80% of total well depth (well depth x 0.8). Where well depth is not recorded, the modeled water table depth at the supply location is used instead. For sites without a well depth on record and without direct raster coverage at their exact location (a water supply point falling just outside the raster extent), the nearest valid modeled value within a progressively expanding search radius (starting at 500 m, doubling up to a 50 km cap) is used instead. Estimated depths greater than 200 m are capped at 200 m before scoring, an analytical saturation point rather than a physical maximum. All other source types are assigned a depth of 0 m because they represent surface-water supplies directly exposed to changing surface-climate conditions.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: shallower depth to water = more vulnerable

data_source: USFS WHP2023 (Dillon et al., 2023); 270 m categorical raster, 5 classes
methodology: Area-weighted percentage of the 4 km water supply buffer in Wildfire Hazard Potential (WHP) categories 4 (high) or 5 (very high). A binary high/very-high raster is derived, and terra::extract(weights=TRUE, exact=TRUE) computes the weighted fraction of the buffer in those classes.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher % high-hazard = more vulnerable

data_source: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL), queried via ArcGIS REST API
methodology: Percentage of the 4 km buffer area within FEMA Special Flood Hazard Areas (zones designated A or V), representing a >=1% annual chance of flooding. Sites with no FEMA data coverage receive NA; sites with FEMA data but no SFHA within the buffer receive 0%. Note that NA here means the site is outside NFHL coverage, not that its flood risk is zero.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher % in flood zone = more vulnerable

data_source: NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer inundation extent rasters with 0 ft of SLR
methodology: Percentage of the 4 km buffer around the water supply that is inundated under present-day (0 ft SLR) conditions. Sites more than 50 km from the shore are assigned NA and excluded from standardization (Jasechko et al., 2020).
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher percentage currently inundated = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 MWBM historical simulation (Alder & USGS, 2023)
methodology: Sen's slope of annual water availability (runoff, for non-rainwater, non-ocean supplies) across the historical period (1980-2010). Annual values are calculated from the LOCA2 MWBM historical simulation and spatially averaged in a 3x3 grid cell window around the water supply grid cell.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative trend (declining water availability) = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 MWBM historical simulation (Alder & USGS, 2023)
methodology: Sen's slope of annual water availability (precipitation, for rainwater-based supplies) across the historical period (1980-2010), spatially averaged in a 3x3 grid cell window around the water supply grid cell.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative trend (declining water availability) = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023)
methodology: Sen's slope of annual mean 12-month SPEI across the historical period (1980-2010). Monthly SPEI is calculated from LOCA2 precipitation and potential evapotranspiration using a 12-month accumulation period. Climate variables are spatially averaged within a 3x3 grid cell window around each water supply before calculating annual mean SPEI and the historical trend.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative trend (increasing drought severity) = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023)
methodology: Sen's slope of annual mean air temperature across the historical period, expressed in degrees Celsius per year. Annual mean temperatures are calculated for each grid cell and then spatially averaged within a 3x3 grid cell window around each water supply before the trend is estimated. This indicator describes ambient climate conditions rather than measured source-water temperature, which is not available nationally. PROVISIONAL: the methodology for this indicator is still under revision and its scores are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: a greater positive warming trend = more vulnerable
